app.subtitle: A virtual molecular dynamics laboratory for computational materials science courses. Set up the system in the left panel, run it, then watch the atoms move and follow their thermodynamic properties.
preset.label: Initial phase
preset.help: Choosing a phase fills in a suitable density and temperature.
side.lattice_help: Number of particles N = side × side. Above 15 × 15 the simulation becomes noticeably slower.
msg.rcut_error: The cutoff r_c* = {rc} is larger than half the box length ({half}). Add more particles or reduce r_c*.
msg.empty: Choose an initial phase in the left panel, then press **Run simulation**. For a first try, the default settings (liquid, 100 particles) finish in a few seconds.
msg.unstable: The simulation became unstable at step {step}. Reduce the time step (Δt*) or lower the density.
anim.box: The simulation box measures {Lx} σ × {Ly} σ (≈ {Ax} × {Ay} Å for {el}) with periodic boundary conditions. An atom leaving one side re-enters from the opposite side.
anim.colour: Colour shows atomic speed. In the solid, atoms only vibrate around their lattice sites. In the liquid, atoms change places but stay close together. In the gas, atoms move freely and rarely collide.
energy.nve_note: Relative fluctuation of the total energy: **{pct} %**. In the NVE ensemble the total energy should be constant. If it fluctuates strongly or keeps rising, the time step Δt* is too large for the velocity Verlet integrator.
energy.nvt_note: With a thermostat the total energy is no longer constant, because the system exchanges energy with a heat bath. What is controlled is the mean temperature, as in the NVT ensemble.
rdf.note: The first peak of g(r) lies at r ≈ **{r} σ** with height **{g}**. Sharp peaks repeating to long distances indicate long range order (solid). Peaks that decay after two or three neighbour shells indicate a liquid. A single low peak that quickly approaches 1 indicates a gas.
msd.too_few: Too few stored frames to compute the MSD. Increase the number of steps or reduce the save interval.
msd.label: MSD
msd.solid: Diffusion coefficient **D* ≈ 0**. The MSD does not grow with time because atoms only vibrate in place, which is typical of a solid.
msd.note: Diffusion coefficient from the Einstein relation: **D* = {D}** (≈ {Dar} {unit} on the {el} scale). Because this system is two dimensional, the value cannot be compared directly with experimental data for three dimensional {el}.
speed.note: Although the initial velocities are drawn at random, collisions between atoms drive the speed distribution towards the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. This is one sign that the system has reached thermal equilibrium.
theory.lj_text: The power 12 term represents short range repulsion and the power 6 term represents van der Waals attraction. Interactions are truncated at r_c and the potential is shifted so that it is zero at the cutoff.
theory.eom_title: Equations of motion and the velocity Verlet integrator
theory.units_text: All quantities are expressed in σ (length), ε (energy), m (mass) and τ = σ√(m/ε) (time). For {el}, σ = {sigma} Å and ε/k_B = {epsK} K, so τ ≈ {tau} ps. Hence T* = 1 corresponds to {epsK} K.
worksheet: **Experiment 1. Integrator stability.** Choose the NVE ensemble and the liquid phase. Run with Δt* = 0.001, 0.005, 0.01 and 0.02. Record the relative fluctuation of the total energy in the *Energy and temperature* tab. Plot the fluctuation against Δt* and explain why a time step that is too large ruins the simulation.

**Experiment 2. Recognising phases from structure.** Run the Gas, Liquid and Solid presets. Compare their g(r) curves. Determine the nearest neighbour distance and relate it to the minimum of the Lennard-Jones potential, r = 2^(1/6) σ.

**Experiment 3. Melting.** At ρ* = 0.90 with the Berendsen thermostat, run simulations at T* = 0.4, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3 and 1.6. Record D* and the height of the first g(r) peak at each temperature. In which temperature range do atoms start to change places? For comparison, also try a gradual temperature change from T* = 0.2 to T* = 1.6 and watch the animation. Note: melting in a small two dimensional system is gradual, so there is no sharp energy jump as in a three dimensional solid.

**Experiment 4. Diffusion and activation energy.** At ρ* = 0.70, compute D* for T* = 0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2 and 1.5. Plot ln D* against 1/T* and decide whether the relation follows the Arrhenius equation.

**Experiment 5. Thermal equilibrium.** Compare the speed histogram with the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve for an equilibration fraction of 0 and of 0.5. Why should the initial part of a simulation be discarded from the analysis?
download.text: Thermodynamic data can be processed in Excel or Python. The extended XYZ trajectory can be opened in OVITO for visualisation and further analysis.
common.quantum_warning: {el} is a light atom with strong quantum effects. This classical simulation is not realistic for {el} at low temperature, so results are only qualitative.
common.done_hint: Set the parameters and press **Run simulation**.
quiz.wrong: Not quite. The correct answer is **{ans}**. {explain}
home.variability: These parameters are approximate. The ε values can differ by 10 % or more depending on the experimental data used for fitting, so conversions to real units should be read as estimates.
col.name: Name
m02.drift: Largest energy deviation: Euler **{e}**, velocity Verlet **{v}**.
m02.broke: The Euler integrator failed (atoms passed through the repulsive wall) at t* = {t}.
m03.anim_title: The simulation box and its periodic images
m03.tracked: The red atom is the same atom in the main box and in each of its images.
m04.fluct: Relative temperature fluctuation after equilibration: NVE **{a} %**, NVT **{b} %**. Number of particles: {n}.
m06.result: The first g(r) peak is at r ≈ **{r} σ** ({ra} Å for {el}). First shell coordination number ≈ **{cn}** (perfect lattice: {ideal}).
m06.density: Density ρ* = {rho} corresponds to **{d} g/cm³** for {el}.
lab.dim_note: The free laboratory works in 2D. Choose a square or hexagonal starting lattice.
units.label: Display units
units.help: Reduced units (σ, ε, m) apply to every Lennard-Jones atom. Real units use the parameters of the reference element below.
units.note2d: Note: in a 2D system, density is expressed per unit area (nm⁻²) and pressure as force per unit length (mN/m). These numbers are useful for comparison but cannot be compared directly with 3D experimental data.
m03.conv_hint: Conversion uses the reference element selected in the left panel: {el}.
